question: What is the difference between an AI tool that monitors students during exams and one that grades their exam answers? Are they treated differently?
gold_source: Annex III, points 3(b) and 3(d); Article 6(2); Articles 8-15
gold_answer: They are two different uses listed in Annex III, point 3. Point 3(b) covers systems that evaluate learning outcomes, and point 3(d) covers systems that monitor and detect prohibited behaviour of students during tests. Both are Annex III systems, so both are considered high-risk under Article 6(2) (subject to Article 6(3)), and both have to meet the requirements of Articles 8 to 15. The difference is the purpose of the system, not the set of requirements.

question: If our exam monitoring tool is high-risk, what do we have to do as the provider before we put it on the market, and what does the system itself have to be able to do?
gold_source: Article 8(1); Articles 9-15; Article 16
gold_answer: Article 8(1) says high-risk systems must comply with the requirements of Section 2: risk management (Article 9), data and data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11), record-keeping (Article 12), transparency and instructions for use (Article 13), human oversight (Article 14), and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15). Article 16 lists the provider's obligations: ensure compliance with these requirements (a), put the provider's name and contact address on the system (b), have a quality management system (c, Article 17), keep documentation (d) and logs (e), complete the conformity assessment before placing on the market (f), draw up the EU declaration of conformity (g), affix the CE marking (h), register in the EU database (i), take corrective actions (j), demonstrate conformity on a reasoned request of an authority (k) and meet accessibility requirements (l).

question: Our university customers' proctors might just accept every flag the tool shows. Which requirements are meant to stop that?
gold_source: Article 14(1); Article 14(4), points (b), (c), (d) and (e); Article 13(1); Article 12(1)
gold_answer: Article 14 requires high-risk systems to be designed so that natural persons can oversee them effectively. Under Article 14(4) the person overseeing must be able to stay aware of automation bias, correctly interpret the output, decide to disregard, override or reverse the output, and intervene or stop the system. Article 13(1) requires enough transparency for deployers to interpret and use the output correctly, and Article 12(1) requires automatic logging of events.
